chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Isma'il ibn Marrar, from Yunus — from them (peace be upon them) who said:
Five things are pure (ritually permissible), from those which have benefits for people: the rennet, and the egg, and the wool, and the hair, and the fur.
There is no problem with eating cheese — all of it — whether made by a Muslim or another.
And it is only disliked to eat, besides the rennet, from what is in the vessels of the Magians and the People of the Book, because they do not refrain from carrion and wine.

key_terms.أَهْل الْكِتَاب: People of the Book — Jews and Christians, those possessing revealed scriptures
key_terms.الْإِنْفَحَة: Rennet — the enzyme extracted from the stomach of an animal used for cheese-making; has special leniency in rulings
key_terms.الْمَجُوس: Majus/Magians — Zoroastrians; treated as a separate legal category from People of the Book
key_terms.الْمَيْتَة: Mayta/carrion — an animal that died without proper Islamic slaughter, considered ritually impure
key_terms.ذَكِيَّة: Pure/tazkiya — things that are juridically treated as if from a lawfully slaughtered animal
key_terms.يُكْرَهُ: Makruh — disliked/discouraged in Islamic jurisprudence, not forbidden but inadvisable

ai.seo_question: Is cheese made by non-Muslims permissible in Islam according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from the Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt (peace be upon them) establishes a key jurisprudential ruling: five products extracted from animals — rennet, eggs, wool, hair, and fur — are ritually pure (tazkiyah) even if taken from an animal that was not properly slaughtered. Practically, this permits consuming all varieties of cheese without restriction based solely on who produced it, Muslim or non-Muslim. However, cheese stored in vessels used by Magians or People of the Book carries a separate concern: their lack of care in avoiding carrion and wine contaminates those vessels, making the contents disliked (makruh) with the exception of rennet which has a different ruling.
